en.before:
Hobbes wrote Leviathan in Paris while England was in the middle of the civil war that beheaded its king. He had fled the country with the royalists in 1640 and was tutoring the future Charles II when the book appeared in 1651. The argument is austere and consecutive. Hobbes begins with the smallest unit — a single mind perceiving the world — and works outward, by definitions and deductions, to the largest unit: the artificial body of the state. The first part, 'Of Man,' is a theory of human nature: sensation, imagination, language, reason, the passions, religion, and what life looks like in the absence of any common authority — the famous 'natural condition of mankind,' which Hobbes describes as a state of war of every man against every man, and human life in it as 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.'

The second part, 'Of Commonwealth,' is the constructive argument. To escape the state of nature, men contract with one another to give up their natural right to act on their own judgement and transfer that right to a single sovereign — one man or one assembly — whose word is law. The sovereign is not a party to the contract; the contract is among the subjects themselves to obey whatever the sovereign commands. Hobbes argues from this premise that the sovereign's authority must be absolute and undivided, that there is no right of resistance except where the sovereign fails to protect the subject's life, and that the only check on sovereign power is the moral pressure of the law of nature acting on the sovereign's own conscience.

Parts III and IV apply the same logic to religion and to political theology. Hobbes is determined to leave no scriptural authority outside the civil sovereign; he rereads the Bible, redefines 'the kingdom of God,' and dismantles what he calls the Roman Catholic Church's claim to a temporal jurisdiction independent of the state. The book ends with a Review and Conclusion in which Hobbes adds one more law of nature — that every man is bound to protect the authority that protects him — and defends the whole discourse against the charge of impiety. Leviathan has been the central text of modern political philosophy ever since, the founding work of the social-contract tradition and the most uncompromising case ever made for sovereign authority as the precondition of any tolerable life.

before.title: The state of nature.
before.text: Hobbes's central thought experiment: if there were no common power to keep men in awe, what would life be like? His answer — war of every man against every man, life solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short — is the foundation of everything that follows.
before.angleObjective: I want to follow Hobbes's argument for the state of nature in Chapter 13 — what he claims about human equality, scarcity, and fear — and decide whether his account of life without a sovereign is convincing.

before.title: The covenant.
before.text: Chapters 14–17 build the social contract. Men agree, each with each, to surrender their natural right to act on their own judgement and transfer it to a single sovereign whose word is law. The contract is among the subjects; the sovereign is not a party to it.
before.angleObjective: I want to read the covenant chapters carefully — what Hobbes thinks the parties are agreeing to, what the sovereign is and is not bound by, and what kind of obligation results.

before.title: Absolute sovereignty.
before.text: Part II argues that sovereign power, once instituted, must be absolute and undivided. No right of resistance except where the sovereign fails to protect life. No separation of powers. Read Hobbes's reasons and test them against everything you know about politics since.
before.angleObjective: I want to read Hobbes's case for absolute sovereignty on its own terms — and then weigh it against the constitutional, separation-of-powers tradition that comes after him.

before.title: Religion and the kingdom of darkness.
before.text: Parts III and IV are about church and state. Hobbes rereads scripture to leave every religious authority subordinate to the civil sovereign, and gives the Roman Catholic Church the title 'Kingdom of Darkness.' Modern readers tend to skip these parts. Skip them and you miss what the book is for.
before.angleObjective: I want to read the religious chapters of Leviathan — the reinterpretation of scripture and the polemic against the 'Kingdom of Darkness' — and understand why Hobbes thought the political argument was incomplete without them.

before.title: The Sentence Everyone Knows
before.body: In Chapter 13, after a page and a half of dry argument about how rough natural equality combines with scarcity to produce competition, diffidence, and the pursuit of glory, Hobbes hands his reader the single most quoted sentence in political philosophy. In the state of nature, he writes, 'there is no place for industry, because the fruit thereof is uncertain; and consequently no culture of the earth; no navigation, nor use of the commodities that may be imported by sea; no commodious building; no instruments of moving and removing such things as require much force; no knowledge of the face of the earth; no account of time; no arts; no letters; no society; and which is worst of all, continual fear, and danger of violent death; and the life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' The list has the rhythm of a hammer. It is the picture every later social-contract thinker has had to refute or accommodate, and the dark mirror against which Locke, Rousseau, and Rawls all wrote. It is also, on Hobbes's own terms, an argument from inside the reader: not a historical claim about what once was, but a deduction about what would be the moment the common power lapsed. Modern political philosophy, in the sense in which it differs from ancient, begins with this paragraph.

before.title: The Most Uncompromising Argument for Sovereignty
before.body: Almost everyone who comes to Leviathan comes wanting to find a way around its central conclusion. Hobbes makes that hard. He argues, step by step, that the sovereign's authority cannot be divided (because divided sovereignty is the same as no sovereignty), that it cannot be limited by law (because the sovereign makes the laws), that it cannot be checked by a constituent power (because the subjects have already given up the right to constitute), and that there is no right of resistance except to a direct order to die. He concedes only one point: a subject may not be obliged to do something that defeats the purpose for which sovereignty was instituted — namely, the preservation of the subject's life. Everything else is the sovereign's. This is the position later constitutional thought spent three centuries trying to refute. The arguments worth reading against it — Locke, Spinoza, Rousseau, Hegel, Schmitt, Rawls — are all visibly engaged with Hobbes's text. The reader who has not actually walked through Hobbes's argument is not yet in the conversation.

before.title: Religion Is Not a Sidebar
before.body: Modern editions of Leviathan often advertise Parts I and II as the philosophical core and treat Parts III and IV — 'Of a Christian Commonwealth' and 'Of the Kingdom of Darkness' — as a religious appendix that can be skipped. Hobbes did not write the book that way. Parts III and IV are nearly half the text, and they are where the political argument lands. Hobbes rereads scripture to show that the Israelites' commonwealth was a sovereign state with God as its sovereign, that the New Testament does not establish a separate ecclesiastical authority, and that any priesthood claiming jurisdiction over the conscience of subjects independent of the civil power is, in his term, a 'Kingdom of Darkness.' The Roman Catholic Church is the named target, but the argument cuts at any religious community that claims to bind subjects beyond what the sovereign permits. This is the part of Leviathan that produced the seventeenth-century scandal, the part that was banned in Oxford and burned in some places, and the part without which the political argument has no edge. Hobbes wrote the political theory because he wanted to settle the religious question. The reader who skips Parts III and IV reads the prelude and not the case.
